title: Surprises in time series analysis
author: Rob J Hyndman
date: 26 October 2026
url: robjhyndman.com/uconn2026
abstract: >-
  I will present a statistical framework for identifying anomalies in three time series settings: unusual observations within a single historical series, unusual series within a large collection, and real-time surveillance of incoming data streams.
  In each case, anomalies are identified using a probabilistic approach based on 'surprisal values' --- equal to minus the log (conditional) density of each observation --- with extreme value theory used to model the tail of the surprisal distribution and avoid strong parametric assumptions.
  The methods will be illustrated using the weird package for R, with examples including French and US mortality rates, and pharmaceutical sales.

# Surprisals

## What do we mean by "weird"?

\placefig{0.1}{1.2}{width=2.3cm}{hawkins.jpg}
\begin{textblock}{12.5}(3,1.2)
\begin{block}{}
\emph{an observation which deviates so much from other observations as to arouse suspicion it was generated by a different mechanism.}\hfill (Hawkins, 1980)
\end{block}
\end{textblock}

\begin{textblock}{12.5}(3,4.3)
\begin{itemize}\tightlist
\item Need a model for the ``usual'' mechanism: a density $f$.
\item An anomaly is an observation that is very unlikely under $f$.
\item For time series, $f$ is a \alert{conditional} density, given the past, or given the smooth signal.
\end{itemize}
\end{textblock}

## Surprisals
\fontsize{13}{14}\sf

\begin{alertblock}{Definition: Surprisal}
  The \textbf{surprisal} of an observation $y_i$ drawn from a probability distribution with density $f$ is
  \centerline{$s_i = -\log f(y_i)$}
\end{alertblock}

* "Log scores" in statistics; "surprisal" coined by Tribus (1961).
* Expected surprisal = entropy. Sum of surprisals = $-\log$ likelihood.\pause

### Time series

* $s_t = -\log f(y_t \mid \mathcal{F}_{t-1})$ where $\mathcal{F}_{t-1} = \{y_1,\dots,y_{t-1}\}$
* $-\log L = \sum_t s_t$ (prediction error decomposition)
* Log score for evaluating density forecasts

## Surprisal probabilities: special cases
\vspace*{-0.2cm}

If $f = \text{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$, then $p_i = 2\left[1 - \Phi(|y_i - \mu|/\sigma)\right]$: a two-sided $z$-score test.

```{r}
#| label: fig_normal
#| fig-height: 3.5

tar_read(fig_normal)
```

## Surprisal probabilities: special cases
\vspace*{-0.2cm}

$p_i < \alpha$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ $y_i$ lies outside the $100(1-\alpha)$\% highest density region.

```{r}
#| label: fig_hdr
#| fig-height: 3.5

tar_read(fig_hdr)
```

# Extreme surprisals

## The surprisal distribution
\fontsize{13}{14}\sf

Let $S = -\log f(Y)$ where $Y$ has density $f$, and
$$G(s) = \Pr(S \le s) = \Pr(f(Y) \ge e^{-s}).$$
Then $p_i = 1-G(s_i)$.\pause

* An anomaly is an extreme value of the surprisal distribution.
* It need not be extreme in the sample space of $f$ (e.g., between modes).
* $f$ may be complicated (multimodal, multivariate, conditional), but $G$ is always a univariate distribution on $\R$.\pause
* If $f$ is wrong, the $p_i$ computed from $f$ are wrong.\newline
  But the \alert{upper tail} of the distribution of the computed $s_i$ can still be estimated.

## Three-type theorem for surprisals

**A1: Sub-Gaussian**: $S =-\log f(Y)$ satisfies, for all $\lambda\in\R$, and some $\nu>0$,
$\E \exp\{\lambda (S-\E[S])\}\le \exp\{\lambda^2 \nu^2/2\}$.`\\`{=latex}
**A2: Sub-exponential**: $S$ is sub-exponential with parameters $\nu$ and $b$, i.e.,
$\E \exp\{\lambda(S-\E[S])\} \leq \exp\{\lambda^2\nu^2/ 2\}$ for all $|\lambda|< 1/b$.`\\`{=latex}
**A3: Polynomial**: $|S|$ has polynomial moments of order $p\ge 1$; i.e., $\mathbb{E}[|S|^p] \le C^p$ for some $C>0$ such that $C^p-1>0$.

* A1 satisfied when $f$ has bounded support
* A2 satisfied when $\log f$ unbounded below, and light tails (e.g., Gaussian)
* A3 satisfied when $f$ has heavy tails (e.g., $t$ with df $\ge 3$)

## Three-type theorem for surprisals
\fontsize{13}{14}\selectfont
Let $y_1,\dots,y_n$ be iid from density $f$, $s_i = -\log f(y_i)$, $M_n=\max\{s_1,\dots,s_n\}$, and $S =-\log f(Y)$ where $Y\sim f$.

1. Under A1:
$$
  \sup_{s:s>0}\left|\Pr\left\{\big|M_n-\E[S]\big|\ge \sqrt{2\nu^2 s}+\sqrt{2\nu^2\log(2n)}\right\}-e^{-s}\right|=o(1).
$$
2. Under A2:
$$
  \sup_{s:s>1/b}\left|\Pr\Big\{\big|M_n-\E[S]\big|\ge (2b)s+(2b)\log(2n)\Big\}-e^{-e^{-s}}\right|=o(1).
$$
3. Under A3:
$$
	\sup_{s:s>C}\left|\Pr\Big\{\big|M_n-\E[S]\big|\ge (Csn^{1/p})\Big\}-e^{-s^{-p}}\right|=o(1).
$$

## Three-type theorem for surprisals
\fontsize{14}{15}\sf

* Gaussian-like surprisal tails $\Rightarrow$ maximum surprisal is reversed Weibull
* Exponential surprisal tails $\Rightarrow$ maximum surprisal is Gumbel
* Only polynomial moments $\Rightarrow$ maximum surprisal is Fréchet

\vspace*{0.2cm}

### Corollary (via Pickands--Balkema--de Haan)
\vspace*{-0.3cm}

The upper tail of the surprisal distribution can be approximated by a Generalized Pareto Distribution, \alert{even if the assumed density $f$ is incorrect}, provided one of A1--A3 is satisfied.

## Approximate GPD surprisal probabilities
\fontsize{13}{14}\sf

* $f^*$: the assumed (possibly incorrect) density. Compute $s_i = -\log f^*(y_i)$.
* $u$: the $(1-\beta)$ sample quantile of $\{s_i\}$ (typically $\beta = 0.1$).
* Fit a GPD to the exceedances $s_i - u$, giving density $\hat{g}$ on $(u,\infty)$.
* For $s_i > u$: \quad $\hat{p}_i = \beta \int_{s_i}^\infty \hat{g}(s)\,ds$. \quad For $s_i \le u$, set $\hat{p}_i = \beta$.\pause
* Only needs $f^*$ to get the *ordering* of the extreme surprisals approximately right.
* `surprisals_prob(..., approximation = "gpd")`

## Hampel identifier
\fontsize{13}{14}\sf\vspace*{-0.2cm}
Window of $2w+1$ observations centred on time $t$:\vspace*{-0.8cm}

\begin{align*}
  m_t & = \text{median}(y_{t - w}, \dots, y_{t + w})                 \\
  a_t & = \text{median}(|y_{t - w} - m_t|, \dots, |y_{t + w} - m_t|) \\
  e_t & = (y_t - m_t)/a_t
\end{align*}

- Anomaly if $|e_t| > k/0.6745$\pause
- Implicit model: $y_t \sim \text{N}(\mu_t, \sigma_t^2)$, $\hat\mu_t = m_t$, $\hat\sigma_t = a_t/0.6745$\pause
- Equivalent to surprisal probability threshold of $\alpha = `r sprintf("%.4f", 2*pnorm(-3))`$ for $k = 3$\pause
- Better: use N(0,1) for surprisals of $e_t$, and GPD for their probabilities\pause
- Multiple testing is awkward: the $e_t$ are not independent

## Surprisals from an STL decomposition
\fontsize{14}{15}\sf

Local medians fail with seasonality. Replace by a better signal estimate.

* STL: $y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t$ (Cleveland et al., 1990; Bandara et al., 2025)
* $m_t = T_t + S_t$, residual $R_t = y_t - m_t$
* $a_t$: robust $Q_n$ scale estimate of $\{R_t\}$, separately for each age group
* $e_t = R_t / a_t$; surprisals under N(0,1), probabilities from GPD

## Surprisals from an STL decomposition

```{r}
#| label: stl-stmf
#| echo: true

stmf_scores <- us_stmf |>
  model(stl = STL(Mortality)) |>
  augment() |>
  group_by(`Age group`) |>
  mutate(e = .resid / robustbase::s_Qn(.resid)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    prob = surprisals_prob(e, distribution = dist_normal(), approximation = "gpd")
  )
```

## US weekly mortality rates

```{r}
#| label: stmf_anomalies
#| echo: true

stmf_scores |>
  filter(prob < 0.02) |>
  arrange(prob) |>
  select(Week, `Age group`, Mortality, .fitted, e, prob)
```

## US weekly mortality rates

```{r}
#| label: fig_stl_anomalies

us_stmf |>

  facet_grid(`Age group` ~ ., scales = "free_y") +
  geom_point(data = stmf_scores |> filter(prob < 0.02), colour = "#C14b14") +
```

## US weekly mortality rates
\fontsize{13}{14}\sf

Four anomalous peaks, each a major COVID-19 wave:

* 2020 W14--W18: first wave (New York, April 2020): all adult age groups
* 2020 W49--2021 W03: winter 2020--21: mostly 65+
* 2021 W33--W39: Delta: only 15--64 and 65--74 (older people vaccinated)
* 2022 W02--W05: Omicron: mostly 65+

## US weekly mortality rates

Low anomalies in 2020 W03--W04 (75+) are an \alert{artefact}:

* rates almost identical to the same weeks of 2019
* STL trend pulled upwards by the COVID-19 peak a few weeks later
* not flagged if STL is fitted only to data up to early March 2020

## Multivariate time series: first PC

```{r}
#| label: us_stmf_pcs
#| echo: true

us_wide <- us_stmf |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(logm = log(Mortality)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    id_cols = Week, names_from = `Age group`, values_from = logm
  )
pcs <- us_wide |>
  select(-Week) |>
  prcomp(rank = 1) |>
  broom::augment(us_wide |> select(Week))
pc_anomalies <- pcs |>
  as_tsibble(index = Week) |>
  model(stl = STL(.fittedPC1)) |>
  augment() |>
  mutate(prob = surprisals_prob(.resid,
    distribution = dist_normal(), approximation = "gpd")) |>
  filter(prob < 0.05)
```

# Weird series

## Feature-based anomaly detection
\fontsize{14}{15.5}\sf

* Comparing whole time series directly is awkward: different scales, lengths, and offsets.
* Summarise each series by a vector of \alert{features}: strength of trend and seasonality, autocorrelations, spectral entropy, level shifts, \dots
* Each series becomes a point in $\R^d$. A weird series is a multivariate anomaly in feature space.
* Most features are scale-free, so series are flagged for their shape and dynamics, not their size.
* A series that is unusual in a way not captured by any feature will not be found.

## Kernel density surprisals
\fontsize{13}{14}\sf\vspace*{-0.3cm}

\begin{block}{KDE}
\centerline{$\symbf{y}_{i} \in \R^d$, \quad $\displaystyle\hat{f}(\symbf{y}) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n |\symbf{H}|^{-1/2} K\big(\symbf{H}^{-1/2}(\symbf{y} - \symbf{y}_i)\big)$}
\end{block}\vspace*{-0.25cm}

* $K$: spherically symmetric kernel; $\symbf{H}$: $d\times d$ bandwidth matrix.
* Each observation inflates its own density estimate: use leave-one-out.

\pause

### LOO KDE values

\centerline{$\displaystyle \hat{f}_{-i}(\symbf{y}_i) = \frac{1}{n-1} \big( n \hat{f}(\symbf{y}_i) - |\symbf{H}|^{-1/2} K(\symbf{0}) \big)$}

* Surprisals $s_i = -\log \hat{f}_{-i}(\symbf{y}_i)$; probabilities from the GPD.

## Australian Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme

```{r}
#| label: weirdseries_kde
#| echo: true

  mutate(
    prob = surprisals_prob(
      PBS_prcomp |> select(.fittedPC1, .fittedPC2),
      loo = TRUE, approximation = "gpd"
    )
  ) |>
  select(Concession, Type, ATC2, .fittedPC1, .fittedPC2, prob) |>
  arrange(prob) |>
```

## Surveillance using forecast distributions
\fontsize{14}{15}\sf

For each $t = I, I+1, \dots$, and each series $i = 1,\dots,M$:

* Fit a model to $y_{i,1},\dots,y_{i,t}$ giving one-step forecast density
  $f_{i,t+1}(y \mid \mathcal{F}_{i,t})$
* Surprisal: $s_{i,t+1} = -\log f_{i,t+1}(y_{i,t+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_{i,t})$
* Surprisal probability: $p_{i,t+1} = \Pr(S \ge s_{i,t+1})$, where\newline $S = -\log f_{i,t+1}(Y \mid \mathcal{F}_{i,t})$ and $Y \sim f_{i,t+1}$
* Start at $I = 36$ (3 years), one-step ETS forecasts, rolling origin.

## Rolling origin one-step forecasts

```{r}
#| label: fig_tscv
#| fig-height: 3.5

tscv_plot(.init = 8, .step = 1, h = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 9, y = 0, label = "h = 1", colour = "#c14b14")
```

## Surveillance using forecast distributions

* If $f_{i,t+1}$ is the true conditional density, and $G_{i,t+1}$ is continuous, then
  $$p_{i,t+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_{i,t} \sim \text{U}(0,1)$$
  so the $p_{i,t}$ are iid U(0,1) over $t$ (a PIT of the surprisals).\pause
* Thresholding at $\alpha$ gives a false alarm rate of $\alpha$ per series per period.\pause
* Model updated each period, so a level shift is flagged when it happens, then becomes the "new normal".\pause
* ETS: Gaussian forecast distributions, so $p_{i,t+1}$ is a two-sided $z$-test on the one-step forecast error.

## A first iteration: $t = 36$

```{r}
#| label: pbsfc
#| echo: true

pbs_fc <- pbs |>
  filter(t <= 36) |>
  group_by_key() |>
  filter(cumsum(Scripts) > 0, n() >= 36) |>
  ungroup() |>
  model(ets = ETS(Scripts)) |>
  forecast(h = 1)
```

## A first iteration: $t = 36$

```{r}
#| label: pbsfc_compare
#| echo: true

pbs_fc |>
  rename(fcast = Scripts) |>
  left_join(pbs |> filter(t == 37), by = c("Month", "ATC2")) |>
  mutate(prob = surprisals_prob(Scripts, distribution = fcast)) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(ATC2, Scripts, fcast, prob) |>
  arrange(prob) |>
  print(n = 5, width = Inf)
```

## Rolling forward through the data

```{r}
#| label: pbsloop
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

pbs$prob <- NA_real_
for (i in seq(36, max(pbs$t) - 1)) {
  pbs_fc <- pbs |>
    filter(t <= i) |>
    group_by_key() |>
    filter(cumsum(Scripts) > 0, n() >= 36) |>
    ungroup() |>
    model(ets = ETS(Scripts)) |>
    forecast(h = 1)
  # ... compute surprisals_prob() for time i+1 and store in pbs$prob
}
```

```{r}
#| label: pbs_scores

pbs_scores <- tar_read(pbs_scores)
pbs_anomalies <- pbs_scores |> filter(prob < 0.001)
```

* `r NROW(pbs_anomalies)` observations with $p_{i,t} < 0.001$, out of `r sum(!is.na(pbs_scores$prob))`.

## Surveillance across several series
\fontsize{14}{15}\sf

Some events affect many series at once: mildly unusual in each, very unusual together.

* $M_t$: number of series monitored at time $t$
* $N_t$: number of series with $p_{i,t} < 0.001$
* If series independent, each flagged with probability $\pi$:\newline
  $N_t \sim \text{Binomial}(M_t, \pi)$; compute $\Pr(N_t \ge n_t)$\pause
* If forecast densities were correct, $\pi = 0.001$.
* But ETS forecast distributions are too narrow: `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(pbs_scores$prob < 0.001, na.rm = TRUE))`% of observations have $p_{i,t} < 0.001$.
* So estimate $\pi$ in real time from all previous months.

## Surveillance across several series

```{r}
#| label: pbs_joint

pbs_joint <- pbs_scores |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(!is.na(prob)) |>
  group_by(Month) |>
  summarise(M = n(), n = sum(prob < 0.001), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(
    pi = (cumsum(n) - n) / (cumsum(M) - M),
    prob = pbinom(n - 1, M, pi, lower.tail = FALSE)
  ) |>
  filter(row_number() > 12)
pbs_joint |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = n)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = prob < 0.001), show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey35", `TRUE` = "#C14b14")) +
  scale_x_yearmonth(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(y = "Number of flagged ATC groups")
```

## Surveillance across several series
\fontsize{12}{13}\sf

```{r}
#| label: pbs_joint_table

pbs_joint |>
  filter(prob < 0.001) |>
  mutate(
    Month = format(Month),
    pi = sprintf("%.4f", pi),
    prob = sprintf("%.1e", prob)
  ) |>
  rename(
    `$M_t$` = M, `$n_t$` = n, `$\\hat\\pi_t$` = pi, `$\\Pr(N_t \\ge n_t)$` = prob
  ) |>
  kableExtra::kbl(booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", escape = FALSE, align = "lrrrr")
feb08 <- pbs_joint |> filter(Month == yearmonth("2008 Feb"))
```

* Dec 1997, Dec 2001: unusually large end-of-year stockpiling spikes
* Mar 1999: no obvious explanation
* Feb 2008: `r feb08$n` of `r feb08$M` groups flagged. Usual February fall did not occur, but Jan + Feb in line with previous years. A change in timing, not demand.\pause
* Independence is unrealistic, so these probabilities are too small. Still useful for ranking months.

# Summary

## Summary
\fontsize{14}{16}\sf

* \alert{Weird times}: remove the signal (moving median, STL), then surprisals of standardised residuals. Check for artefacts near large anomalies.
* \alert{Weird series}: features $\rightarrow$ multivariate anomaly detection, using LOO KDE surprisals.
* \alert{Surveillance}: surprisals of one-step forecast densities, refitting as data arrive. Forecast distributions are often too narrow.
* In every case: surprisal = $-\log$(conditional density); extreme surprisals have an approximate GPD tail even when $f$ is wrong.
